Medical History

- Current health issues and chronic disease risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes):  History of asthma with current 2–3-day flare (wheeze, exertional dyspnoea, dry cough); atopic conditions (hay fever, eczema); no smoking; mild alcohol intake; no other chronic conditions recorded.  
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes):  Not recorded.  
- Current medications including OTC and traditional medicines:  Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented; patient reports PRN use every few weeks and before exercise); no other regular or OTC/traditional medicines.  
- Immunisation status reviewed (flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal, shingles, tetanus):  Not recorded.  
- Sexual/reproductive health status and risks:  Not recorded.  
- Lifestyle: physical activity, diet, tobacco, alcohol, substance use:  • Normally walks to work; currently reduced activity due to breathlessness.  • Non-smoker.  • Alcohol: ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days.  • Diet and other substances: not recorded.

- Mood, mental health, and risk assessment (depression, anxiety, self-harm):  Not recorded.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 33-year-old with known asthma, presenting with 2–3-day history of wheeze, dyspnoea on exertion, dry cough, subjective fever (objective 37 °C).  
• No chest pain, haemoptysis, nocturnal symptoms, or smoking history.  
• Past atopy (hay fever, eczema).  
• Telehealth—no objective lung exam or peak flow available.

Working diagnosis  
Acute asthma exacerbation, likely triggered by viral upper-respiratory infection or seasonal allergens.

Supporting DDx evidence  
– Consistent history of asthma and classic symptoms (High likelihood).  
– Viral infection/acute bronchitis (Medium likelihood) may be concurrent trigger.  
– Allergic (pollen-induced) flare (Medium likelihood) given atopy history.

Management/plan  
• Increase salbutamol to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours PRN via newly prescribed spacer.  
• Prescribe peak-flow meter; record measurements morning and evening for one week.  
• Recommend daily oral antihistamine (OTC) for hay fever.  
• Safety-net: call clinic if fever develops or wheeze/shortness of breath worsens.  
• Arrange follow-up tele-review in one week to assess symptoms and peak-flow diary; consider controller inhaler initiation at that visit.  
• Pharmacist to provide inhaler technique education and spacer demonstration.

Considerations  
• Viral respiratory infection / acute bronchitis.  
• Allergic asthma flare.  
• Pulmonary embolism and pneumonia considered low likelihood based on current data.

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification:  Provided advice on proper inhaler use, spacer technique, peak-flow monitoring, trigger avoidance; encouraged prompt review if symptoms escalate.  
- Patient health goals and priorities:  Return to baseline activity and work; improve asthma control.  
- Eligibility for GP Management Plan (GPMP) or Team Care Arrangements (TCA):  Not recorded.  
- Referrals (allied health, Quitline, AOD services, Aboriginal health worker, or social supports):  Pharmacist for spacer/technique and peak-flow education.  
- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled:  Review in 1 week; earlier if deterioration.  

Consider

- Mental health support or counselling referral:  Mental health concerns not identified; support not arranged.  
- Specialist referral for complex chronic disease management:  Consider respiratory specialist if poor control at follow-up (not yet initiated).  
- Dental referral if oral health issues identified:  Not recorded.  
- Optometry referral for visual concerns or regular screening:  Not recorded.  
- Audiometry referral if hearing issues suspected:  Not recorded.  
- Social work or housing support referral if social determinants affect health:  Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute asthma exacerbation – High likelihood: established asthma history, classic wheeze/dyspnoea, precipitating viral/allergic trigger, good response plan.  
2. Viral respiratory infection / acute bronchitis – Medium likelihood: acute onset, cough, mild subjective fever; could trigger asthma.  
3. Allergic (pollen-induced) asthma flare – Medium likelihood: atopic background, seasonal possibility, respiratory-only presentation.

Quality checks

● Missing but clinically expected elements: BP, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, BMI, immunisation review, lipid/glucose screening, foot/eye checks, urinalysis.  
● Internal conflicts or contradictions: None significant; patient reported fever but objective temp normal.  
● Transcript quality notes: Telephone consultation—no physical exam; some patient recall limited (medication names, past asthma timeline).
